summary:
This evaluation covered four chat-task evals related to EC2/SSM Patch Manager reboot handling, three of which were actively scored (the fourth, "unrelated-question," was skipped entirely since it tests a should-not-trigger scenario, so no data exists there).

**Trigger firing**: In all three scored evals, the behavior under test fired 100% of the time (3/3) for the shared trigger metric — this is not a differentiator since it's not measured per-variant.

**Expected output / assertions**: This is where the two variants diverge most clearly:
- "pending-reboot-not-a-failure": with_skill met expected output 3/3 (high confidence) and passed all 15/15 assertions; without_skill also met expected output 3/3 but only on medium confidence, and passed just 6/15 assertions. Two assertions passed for both (always_passes — not differentiating), but three assertions passed only for with_skill (controlled-reboot language, change-window recommendation, NoReboot policy explanation), all at high confidence on both sides.
- "reboot-race-bounded-wait": both variants matched expected output at 2/3 (with_skill high confidence, without_skill medium). Assertion pass rates: with_skill 10/10, without_skill 11/15 (73%). Three assertions always passed for both. One was flaky for without_skill (bounded-wait recommendation, 2/3). One assertion (warning against retrying into a still-rebooting host / connectivity triage) passed for with_skill (2/2) but failed entirely for without_skill (0/3, medium confidence).
- "reboot-gating-rebootoption": with_skill met expected output 3/3 (medium confidence) with 15/15 assertions passing; without_skill failed to meet expected output at all (0/3, high confidence) with only 4/15 assertions passing. Three assertions failed consistently for without_skill (RebootOption terminology, approval/change-window language, gating logic) while passing fully for with_skill. One assertion always passed for both, and one was flaky for without_skill (33%).

Across all three evals, no assertion passed for without_skill alone while failing for with_skill — the asymmetry runs one direction. Several assertions that both variants always passed indicate those specific checks aren't distinguishing the variants.

**Quality comparison**: Results are thin and mixed. In "pending-reboot-not-a-failure," the 3 evaluated pairs split evenly (with_skill and without_skill each favored on 3 sub-judgments, 3 comparable), at medium confidence. In "reboot-race-bounded-wait," only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated (2 skipped), with without_skill favored on 2 criteria and with_skill on 1 — a small, low-coverage sample. In "reboot-gating-rebootoption," all quality pairs were skipped (0 of 3 evaluated), so no quality signal exists there at all. Overall, quality comparisons are sparse and shouldn't be read as a strong signal either way.

**Runtime and cost**: with_skill consistently took ~7-9 seconds and cost ~$0.07-0.08 per eval; without_skill registered ~0 seconds and $0.00 cost in all three evals. This is a notable and consistent pattern, though it stands alongside with_skill's generally higher assertion-pass and expected-output rates — a cost/thoroughness tradeoff rather than a clear verdict. No runs exceeded the 30s runtime threshold for either variant.

**Output consistency across repeated runs**: with_skill was "consistent" in one eval (score 3.0), "mostly_consistent" in another (2.33), and had no data in the third (null, likely due to the single-pair quality evaluation limiting data). without_skill was "mostly_consistent" or "consistent" across its three measured evals (scores 2.33–3.0). Both variants show generally stable but not perfectly uniform outputs across runs, with with_skill's one missing data point representing an absence of data rather than a weakness.

**Overall**: The clearest and most consistent pattern is that with_skill met expected outputs and passed assertions at equal or higher rates than without_skill in all three scored evals, with several specific assertions (RebootOption gating, approval/change-window language, connectivity-triage routing) failing for without_skill but passing reliably for with_skill. Confidence on without_skill's expected-output judgments was medium in two of three evals, suggesting some of this gap rests on less certain judgments. Set against this, without_skill ran faster and at lower reported cost in every eval, and quality-comparison data (where available) was mixed or too sparse to draw firm conclusions, with one eval's quality comparisons entirely skipped. The "unrelated-question" eval contributes no data in either direction since it was skipped as not-applicable.

reboot-race-bounded-wait.summary:
This chat-task eval tested an incident-RCA scenario involving a reboot-timing race during patching. The trigger behavior fired reliably in all 3 runs (not variant-specific).

Expected-output match: both variants matched the expected output in 2 of 3 runs (67%), an identical rate. Confidence in this judgment was high for with_skill and only medium for without_skill, so without_skill's equal-looking score rests on a slightly weaker measurement.

Assertions: with_skill passed all of its evaluated assertion instances (10/10), while without_skill passed 11/15 (73%). Looking at the five underlying assertion types rather than the aggregate: three assertions passed consistently for both variants across all runs (regex checks for race/timing language and for bounded/poll/wait language, and correctly identifying a reboot-timing race) — these aren't differentiating. One assertion ("recommend bounded wait + single retry, not indefinite loop") was flaky for without_skill (2/3) while with_skill passed it every time. One assertion ("warn against retrying into a still-rebooting host and route a never-Online instance to connectivity triage") passed fully for with_skill (2/2) but failed entirely for without_skill (0/3) — a clear and consistent split on this specific behavior, not just a one-off flake.

Quality comparison: only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated head-to-head for quality (2 were skipped), so this is a thin sample. In that single comparable pair, without_skill was favored on accuracy and completeness, while with_skill was favored on actionability; confidence in these judgments was medium. Given only one pair was assessed, this should be treated as a weak signal rather than a robust pattern.

Metrics: with_skill averaged ~7s runtime and ~$0.07 per run, with 4.0% context utilization; without_skill averaged ~0s runtime and ~$0.00 cost, with 3.6% context utilization. No compactions occurred for either. Neither exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the one evaluated runtime pair.

Output consistency: without_skill was rated "consistent" across its 3 runs (score 3.0, high confidence). No consistency score is available for with_skill (null), so no comparison can be made on this dimension — it's missing data for with_skill rather than a negative result.

Overall, this is a mixed picture: equal expected-output match rates (with weaker confidence behind without_skill's score), several assertions that don't differentiate the variants, one flaky assertion favoring with_skill, and one assertion that fails consistently for without_skill but passes consistently for with_skill (the connectivity-triage/retry-warning behavior). Variant_a took measurably longer and cost more per run. The quality comparison is too sparse (1 of 3 pairs) to draw confident conclusions, and consistency data exists only for without_skill.
